title: Neural Networks in Trading: A Spiking Architecture for Spatio-Temporal Market Analysis (Encoder)
text:
Introduction
The market has never stood still. It has always moved to the rhythm of short bursts of activity, lulls, and unexpected reversals. For an experienced practitioner, this scenario has long been a familiar one. A price chart resembles the pulse of a living organism, and the tick stream is a series of barely perceptible signals that appear, disappear, and reappear, creating a complex web of market dynamics. And the more closely we examine these subtle shifts, the clearer it becomes that traditional data processing methods are not always fast enough to keep up with the pace of change in today's market.
Today, the market is moving faster than ever. Information spreads instantly. The algorithms respond with virtually no delay. And the tick stream has become so sparse yet information-rich that it is increasingly difficult to identify stable patterns within it. Traditional neural network architectures, which rely on dense data samples and fixed sampling rates, are beginning to fall short of real-time requirements. They require more memory, more computation, and more averaging, and therefore lose sight of the very essence of what is happening at the micro-event level.
This is where the concept of event-driven data processing originates. It brings us back to a fundamental principle: do not react to everything, but only to signals. If the market speaks, the model must listen. If the market falls silent, the model must remain calm. This approach is closer to the classical concepts of rational observation. We pay attention to the words, not the silence between them.
This is the principle behind the
SDformerFlow
framework, proposed in the research paper "
SDformerFlow: Spatiotemporal swin spikeformer for event-based optical flow estimation
". Its architecture is built around an event-based data representation — sparse but precise. It is designed for streams where every change has meaning. Where there is no regular time grid, but rather a sequence of pulses. Where the density of information changes from moment to moment. It is precisely this type of data that increasingly resembles the structure of a real market data stream.
SDformerFlow
brings together several powerful ideas. First, it uses spiking neural networks, which are naturally well-suited to processing sparse sequences. A spiking neuron responds only when there is something for it to respond to — and this is important when working with financial data, where most ticks do not reflect a significant market move. Second, the architecture is based on transformers with sliding
3D
windows, allowing it to examine dynamics in three dimensions at once: local space, temporal context, and their interactions. This classic multilayer approach makes the model flexible and highly scalable. Local detail captures micro-impulses, while broader patterns emerge at higher levels.
The third advantage is its hierarchical processing structure. In
SDformerFlow
, information is gradually
aggregated
and
condensed
through several levels of
Spiking Patch Merge
, while the time axis remains intact. This has a significant effect. The model can process short time intervals without losing synchronization. This is uncommon in time series analysis. Most architectures sacrifice temporal accuracy for the sake of abstraction; here, however, it is possible to preserve both.
For a financial markets professional, this structure is particularly valuable. It resembles the long-standing tradition of chart analysis. We start with minute-by-minute fluctuations, then look at the broader picture over the course of an hour, a day, or a week.
SDformerFlow
does something similar, but in the world of event data. It constructs signals while preserving context at every level. And if a spike in activity suddenly occurs in the tick stream, the model detects it both at the low level and within the structure of larger patterns.
Another important quality is energy and computational efficiency. Spiking architectures do not waste resources processing empty regions. This is especially important for financial data: the terms
online learning
and
stream processing
are not just buzzwords. They describe a real need. For traders and trading system developers, it is important that the model be lightweight, fast, and run reliably in the trading terminal.
SDformerFlow
, by its very nature, solves this problem elegantly. It works where dense architectures start to slow down.
It is precisely these features that make
SDformerFlow
an interesting tool for the financial markets. The model does not just analyze the price — it hears its rhythm. It takes into account the structure of events, not just averaged candlesticks. It detects local spikes and can distinguish noise from price movement. This approach is particularly consistent with the classical principles of technical analysis. We look for key points and market reactions; we don't calculate continuous functions.
The author's visualization of the
SDformerFlow
framework is shown below.
We aim to implement the proposed architecture using
MQL5
and
OpenCL
, adapting it to the specific requirements of trading. The first phase has already been completed. We analyzed the basic components and laid the groundwork for the future implementation. Now it's time to move on and dive into building the model's key modules. A long and careful exploration of the
SDformerFlow
architecture lies ahead. And every new detail will bring us closer to creating an effective, rationally designed, and readily explainable tool for market analysis.
Attention Module
Now that we have reviewed the key benefits of the
SDformerFlow
framework, it is time to move from general concepts to practical implementation. Today's focus is on building the
STSF
encoder, one of the fundamental components of the entire model. Essentially, it is the workhorse of the framework. This is the component that transforms a sparse stream of events into a structured representation ready for further analysis.
The authors propose building an
STSF
encoder based on three key spiking elements:
multi-head attention in event-based form;
spiking
MLP
;
a compact
Patch-Merging
block that neatly reduces the dimensionality.
This combination looks conventional at first glance — but only until we take a closer look. Here, each module operates on a specific principle. Reactions occur exclusively at moments of significant change. This makes processing rich in information yet computationally lightweight.
The logic behind the design of the
STSF
encoder resembles the work of a craftsperson who, layer by layer, removes the excess and leaves only the most expressive details. Multi-head spiking attention acts as a fine filter. It maintains a local focus, identifies relationships between events, and passes on only what truly affects the dynamics of the stream. A spiking MLP acts as a precise converter, adapting the feature structure for subsequent analysis while keeping the model lightweight. The block ends with
Patch-Merging
— the equivalent of a classic
lens
that gently compresses the space without disrupting the temporal structure of the sequence.
It is worth noting that the framework's authors have left us with an important architectural choice by offering two options for the event-driven attention module. The first option is closer to the classical school of transformers and relies on the
dot-product
mechanism — a precise, time-tested approach. It ensures a high level of model expressiveness, clear relationships between elements in the sequence, and stable behavior even with complex data.
The second option is a lightweight version of attention based on the
QK line attention
principle. Here, the computations are organized so that computational cost scales linearly with the length of the window being analyzed, rather than quadratically as in classical
dot-product
attention. This approach offers a noticeable advantage in long, event-rich streams, where even a small reduction in the computational load translates into a significant speed boost. And although linear attention is less resource-intensive, it retains the ability to identify key relationships in the data. This makes it particularly attractive for real-world trading streams, where the volume of events being analyzed can change several times per second.
As part of our work, we made a well-considered and entirely pragmatic decision to use the second option — linear
QK-attention
. It better aligns with the nature of event streams and allows for high processing speeds without noticeably compromising its ability to capture dependencies. For market data, this reduction in computational load plays a key role. For long sequences, the model must respond as quickly as the price changes.
However, we did not limit ourselves to simply implementing the basic version. Linear attention opens up opportunities for further optimizations, especially in
MQL5
and
OpenCL
environments. We will discuss the changes to the algorithm as we implement it.
Before we move on to constructing a new object and assembling complete linear attention blocks, we need to carry out a small but important preparatory task. Just as in traditional engineering practice, building a complex mechanism begins with debugging basic operations. In our case, we are talking about one of the fundamental operations on which a significant portion of the arithmetic in linear
QK-attention
is based — scalar-vector multiplication.
At first glance, this is an extremely simple operation — almost trivial. However, in an event-driven architecture, where computations are performed in streaming mode, it is used so frequently that even the slightest optimization noticeably increases the encoder's overall processing speed. That is precisely why we move it to the
OpenCL
context level and implement it as a separate, high-performance kernel. This approach reduces the load on the model's central logic and offloads routine computations to the
GPU
, where they can be naturally parallelized.
To do this, we create a compact yet efficient
ScalarToVector
kernel that performs element-wise multiplication of the input vector by a scalar.
__kernel
void
ScalarToVector(__global
const
float
* scalar,

const
float

                             __global
float

const
size_t vec = get_global_id(

const
size_t vectors = get_global_size(

);
const
size_t dimension = get_global_size(
1
);
//---
float
sc = IsNaNOrInf(scalar[vec],
0.0
f);
int
shift = RCtoFlat(vec, d, vectors, dimension,
0
);
float
v = IsNaNOrInf(vector_in[shift],
0.0
f);
//---
vector_out[shift] = IsNaNOrInf(sc * v,
0.0
f);

The structure is clear and strictly linear. Each work-item processes its own pair of indices, retrieves the scalar value, handles potentially invalid input data using
IsNaNOrInf
, multiplies the scalar by the corresponding vector element, and writes the result to the output buffer.
This function will serve as a building block for future computational chains. It will allow us to quickly scale operations on feature vectors.
Along with the forward pass, we need to implement the error backpropagation mechanism right away. In trainable models, every operation must have a backward counterpart that allows gradients to be correctly propagated to the preceding layers. This is especially important for linear attention, where even simple operations are part of long computation chains. Failing to compute gradients at such an early stage means leaving a gap that will later result in incorrect weight updates and a loss of convergence.
The backpropagation algorithm in the
ScalarToVectorGrad
kernel is surprisingly simple and, at the same time, elegant. It is like a good old-fashioned clock mechanism, where every cog works toward the common goal.
__kernel
void
ScalarToVectorGrad(__global
const
float
* scalar,
                                 __global
float
* scalar_gr,
                                 __global
const
float
* vector_in,
                                 __global
float
* vector_in_gr,
                                 __global
float
* vector_out_gr,
const
int
dimension
                                )
  {
const
size_t vec = get_global_id(
0
);
const
size_t loc  = get_local_id(
1
);
const
size_t vectors = get_global_size(
0
);
const
size_t total_loc = get_local_size(
1
);
//---
__local
float
temp[LOCAL_ARRAY_SIZE];
At the very beginning, each thread determines its own scope of work: the vector's index in the batch, the thread's position within the work-group, and the number of threads that collectively process the same vector. This sets the pace for the entire computation, allowing the load to be distributed evenly.
To avoid repeatedly accessing global memory, one thread preloads the scalar into a temporary local buffer. The synchronization barrier forces the other threads to wait a moment until the value is in place, after which each participant gains quick access to it, just as if it were a shared reference book lying in the middle of the table.
if
(loc ==
0
)
      temp[
0
] = IsNaNOrInf(scalar[vec],
0.0
f);
   BarrierLoc
float
sc = temp[
0
];
float
sc_gr =
0
;
Next comes the main work: each thread handles several vector coordinates assigned according to its index within the group, iterating through them step by step to the end of the vector. This ensures massive parallelism, where each thread is responsible for its own part of the computation.
for
(
int
d = loc; d < dimension; d += total_loc)
     {
int
shift = RCtoFlat(vec, d, vectors, dimension,
0
);
float
v = IsNaNOrInf(vector_in[shift],
0.0
f);
float
grad = IsNaNOrInf(vector_out_gr[shift],
0.0
f);
      vector_in_gr[shift] = IsNaNOrInf(grad * sc,
0.0
f);
      sc_gr += IsNaNOrInf(v * grad,
0.0
f);
     }
At each of these steps, three key actions take place. First, the thread retrieves the next vector element from the input array, along with the gradient of the output value. It then immediately computes the gradient with respect to the input element itself by simply multiplying the output gradient by the stored scalar. Finally, in parallel with this, the thread begins accumulating its contribution to the gradient with respect to the scalar. This contribution is always simple: the product of the input value and the output gradient. As a result, each thread produces a small
portion
of the total sum.
Once the group members have finished iterating over their elements, it is time to combine the accumulated results. The entire work-group uses a simple reduction procedure: each thread places its partial sum into a local buffer, and then the values are added together in the standard way until a single final value remains. It is equally accessible to all threads, but only one thread — the one responsible for writing the final gradient with respect to the scalar for the current vector — should write it to the global array.
sc_gr = LocalSum(sc_gr,
1
, temp);
if
(loc ==
0
)
      scalar_gr[vec] = sc_gr;
  }
The kernel then finishes execution smoothly, leaving behind two neatly filled arrays. The first contains the gradients with respect to the input vector, computed elementwise and stored at the same indices as the original data. The second is the gradient with respect to the scalar, computed through the combined work of all threads in the work-group. The entire procedure runs smoothly, predictably, and efficiently, ensuring correct error backpropagation for scalar-vector multiplication and making it suitable for large-scale neural network computations within future
STSF
encoder modules.
Here, we are entering a new, more significant phase of implementation. After a small but essential amount of preparatory work in the
OpenCL
program, we can build the first fully fledged computational module — the
CNeuronSpikeQKAttention
object. The structure looks massive and multi-layered, but inside it follows a strict logic, like a well-designed machine where every part has its own specific function.

The class structure shown here declares a number of auxiliary components. The
cQK
and
cSpikeQK
pair is responsible for generating preliminary spiking representations for queries and keys, creating the dense, efficient encoding that makes the entire framework unique.
Next come two basic objects —
cQ
and
cK
— which essentially represent separate channels for generating
Q
and
K
. Next comes the
cScore
block, which uses multi-channel convolution to produce a matrix of
attention logits
. The
cSpikeScore
block supplements these calculations with spiking activation, helping to produce a more expressive, energy-efficient response. The
cProject
module completes the chain by bringing the results together and generating the final multidimensional representation.
The initialization method carefully constructs the internal geometry of the entire object and ensures that every component is ready for use within the
OpenCL
context.

First, the parent class's initialization method is called. Here, the neuron's
main resources
are created, taking into account the total number of results and a pointer to the
OpenCL

false
, protecting the system from an invalid state.
Next, the internal blocks are initialized in stages. The
cQK
block is the heart of the
QK
attention mechanism, where the kernels for generating
Q
and
K
are created. We pass the window size, the number of neurons, and the sizes along the key dimensions.

;

The
cQ
and
cK
objects each receive
half of the neurons
from

and

;

if

0

false
;

Next,
an array of windows
is created according to the specified number of attention heads, and the attention computation block is initialized.

windows[];

int
)heads)

;

Each attention head is assigned its own window of dimension
dimension_k
.
It is worth noting that in the original version of the
SDformerFlow
framework, the authors simply sum the elements of the query vector (
Query
) when calculating the score. We took it a step further and implemented
weighted summation with trainable coefficients
, which allows each component of the vector to make its own individual contribution to the final value.
In addition, integrating
the multi-window convolution object
makes it possible to train separate parameters for each attention head. This opens up opportunities for more flexible and adaptive model configuration. Each attention head can account for different characteristics of the signal and develop its own combinations of weights. As a result, the algorithm becomes
more sensitive to the data structure
and more accurate in its predictions, while maintaining overall compactness and computational efficiency.
The next step is to create a spiking layer for scoring. It converts the results into spikes that define masks for the key tensor.
index++;
if
(!cSpikeScore.Init(
0
, index, OpenCL, cScore.Neurons(), optimization, iBatch))
return
false
;
Next, the projection block is prepared: it is cleared and granted access to
OpenCL
.
cProject.Clear();
   cProject.SetOpenCL(OpenCL);
The first object in the projection module is the base neural layer, in which we will store the results of multiplying the key tensor by the attention mask.
index++;
   CNeuronBaseOCL* neuron =
new
CNeuronBaseOCL();
if
(!neuron ||
      !neuron.Init(
0
, index, OpenCL, cK.Neurons(), optimization, iBatch) ||

return

;

The method concludes with the initialization of
the convolutional block

, optimization, iBatch) ||

;

This block aggregates signals by combining all attention heads into a single structure.
After successfully adding all components, the method returns
true
, indicating that the object is fully ready.
As a result, the initialization method carefully constructs a coherent, multilevel attention structure based on spiking neurons. Each block is initialized according to a strict geometric layout, the activation functions are synchronized, and error checking at every step ensures stability. This sequence of steps transforms a potentially chaotic set of components into an organized, flexible architecture that is ready for training and processing streaming data.
The
feedForward
method is responsible for
processing the input data stream step by step
and converting it into a neatly organized structure of attention signals. Unlike the standard implementation of the framework, where the elements of the query vector are simply summed, we use weighted summation with trainable coefficients, which allows each component of the
Q
vector to make an individual contribution. This gives the algorithm the flexibility and precision to adapt to the characteristics of the input signal.
bool
CNeuronSpikeQKAttention::feedForward(CNeuronBaseOCL *NeuronOCL)
  {
if
(!cQK.FeedForward(NeuronOCL))
return
false
;
First, the signal under analysis is fed into the
QK
block, which forms kernels for generating the
Q
and
K
vectors, laying the foundation for attention.
The signal is then converted into spiking activity using
cSpikeQK
.
uint
units = cQK.GetUnits();
uint
window = cQK.GetWindow();
uint
dimension_k = cScore.GetWindow(
0
);
uint
hd = cQK.GetFilters() /
2
;
uint
heads = hd / dimension_k;
//---
if
(!cSpikeQK.FeedForward(cQK.AsObject()))
return
false
;
if
(!DeConcat(cQ.getOutput(), cK.getOutput(), cSpikeQK.getOutput(), hd, hd, units))
return
false
;
After that, the combined output is split into separate
Query
and
Key
entities. This step ensures that the data for each attention head is precisely aligned, guaranteeing signal consistency at all levels.
The next step is to compute the scores. The vector
Q
passes through the multi-window convolutional block
cScore
, where weighted summation is performed using individual parameters for each attention head.
if
(!cScore.FeedForward(cQ.AsObject()))
return
false
;
if
(!cSpikeScore.FeedForward(cScore.AsObject()))
return
false
;
Each attention head can adapt to distinct characteristics of the stream being analyzed, making the model sensitive to local data structures.
The scoring results are then converted into spikes using
cSpikeScore
.
After that, the scalar scores are multiplied by the
K
vectors, producing a consistent output for each attention head.
CNeuronBaseOCL* neuron = cProject[
0
];
if
(!neuron ||
      !ScalarToVector(cSpikeScore.getOutput(), cK.getOutput(), neuron.getOutput(), dimension_k))
return
false
;
Next, each neuron in the projection block processes the signal from the previous one, creating a chain of transformations that carefully aggregate the data stream and form the final result tensor.
for
(
int
i =
1
; i < cProject.Total(); i++)
     {
      neuron = cProject[i];
if
(!neuron ||
         !neuron.FeedForward(cProject[i -
1
]))
return
false
;
     }
The final step is to add the residual connections. The outputs of the projection block are added to the input data.
if
(!SumAndNormilize(NeuronOCL.getOutput(), neuron.getOutput(), Output, window,
false
,
0
,
0
,
0
,
1
))
return
false
;
//---
return
true
;
  }
Thus, our forward pass method creates an adaptive, learnable attention mechanism. Each attention head has its own parameters, and the query vector is formed taking into account the individual influence of each element. This makes the algorithm more accurate and sensitive to the characteristics of time series, which is particularly important for processing highly dynamic financial streams with unpredictable structures.
The
calcInputGradients
method is responsible for backpropagating the error through all components of the object. Its task is to accurately compute the gradients for each element and prepare the network for weight adjustment, ensuring that the model is trained accurately.
bool
CNeuronSpikeQKAttention::calcInputGradients(CNeuronBaseOCL *NeuronOCL)
  {
if
(!NeuronOCL)
return
false
;
//---
uint
units = cQK.GetUnits();
uint
window = cQK.GetWindow();
uint
dimension_k = cScore.GetWindow(
0
);
uint
hd = cQK.GetFilters() /
2
;
uint
heads = hd / dimension_k;
First, the method checks the validity of the received pointer to the input neuron object. If the object is missing, further calculations are not possible. This is a basic safeguard that ensures stability.
Next, the structure's parameters are retrieved. They are needed to ensure that the dimensions of the signals and gradients match exactly at all levels of the model.
The next step is to work with the projection block (
cProject
). Here, the error gradient received from downstream model objects is adjusted using the derivative of the activation function of the final projection layer.
CNeuronBaseOCL* neuron = cProject[-
1
];
if
(!neuron ||
      !DeActivation(neuron.getOutput(), neuron.getGradient(), Gradient, neuron.Activation()))
return
false
;
This restores the correct gradients, which will be used to calculate the errors in the previous layers.
Next, starting with the second-to-last neuron, backpropagation of the error is performed across all layers of the projection.
for
(
int
i = cProject.Total() -
2
; i >=
0
; i--)
     {
      neuron = cProject[i];
if
(!neuron ||
         !neuron.CalcHiddenGradients(cProject[i +
1
]))
return
false
;
     }
Each neuron receives gradients from the next layer, forming a chain of correct signal adjustments from output to input.
Next, we split the gradients between the scoring block and the vector space of the
K
block.
if
(!ScalarToVectorGrad(cSpikeScore.getOutput(), cSpikeScore.getGradient(),
                          cK.getOutput(), cK.getGradient(),
                          neuron.getGradient(), dimension_k))
return
false
;
The method carefully distributes the error to the scoring block and individual neurons of the
K
block, taking into account the weighted parameters we used in
feedForward
. This is a key point for adaptive learning. Each attention head receives individual gradient signals.
The next steps are backpropagation through the
Q
and
Score
blocks.
if
(!cScore.CalcHiddenGradients(cSpikeScore.AsObject()))
return
false
;
if
(!cQ.CalcHiddenGradients(cScore.AsObject()))
return
false
;

Conclusion
We examined in detail the design and integration of a spiking attention block with a residual
MLP
architecture within the
STSF
block. We demonstrated how using weighted summation of
Query
and multi-window convolution for each attention head improves the algorithm's adaptability and the accuracy of streaming data processing. The
CNeuronSDSA
implementation combines the stability of the
MSRes
block with the flexibility of spiking attention, creating a unified mechanism capable of identifying local and global dependencies.
In the next article, we will continue our work by focusing on testing, performance evaluation, and the practical application of the approaches we have implemented, which will allow us to fully realize the potential of the
SDformerFlow
framework.

for: The framework uses spiking neural networks, which respond only when there is something significant — matching the sparse, event-driven nature of tick data where most ticks do not reflect meaningful market moves

It implements linear QK-attention with computational cost scaling linearly (not quadratically) with window length — enabling high-speed processing of long, event-rich streams where 'even a small reduction in computational load translates into a significant speed boost'

The authors replaced the original SDformerFlow's simple sum of query vector elements with 'weighted summation with trainable coefficients', allowing each component of the Q vector to make its own individual contribution — increasing sensitivity to data structure and prediction accuracy

Multi-window convolution is used with separate trainable parameters per attention head — enabling each head to 'account for different characteristics of the signal' and 'develop its own combinations of weights'

The architecture preserves temporal structure while aggregating information hierarchically via 'Spiking Patch Merge', allowing it to 'process short time intervals without losing synchronization' — unlike most time series models that 'sacrifice temporal accuracy for abstraction'
